fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Renaissance as a forgery workshop", "body": "Chance Garton frames the whole conversation around a claim that sounds wild until you follow the paper trail. The Renaissance is taught as a rediscovery of classical culture, but he argues it may be better described as the invention of the idea of classical culture. Ancient artifacts and manuscripts became a fad, and there was obvious motivation to manufacture them for money and reputation. He is careful to flag the fallacy of appeal to motivation, then points out that the motive was real anyway, and that what he covers here is only the tip of the iceberg."}, {"title": "Dylan reads the alphabets and catches the fraud", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio credits other researchers for most of the forgery discoveries, saying his own contribution came from years of reading old texts and learning Hebrew, Greek, Phoenician, Etruscan and other early alphabetical systems. Once you know which letters a culture actually had at a given time, a supposedly ancient inscription that uses letters invented centuries later exposes itself. His example is stele claimed to be Phoenician that use a letter like cough, the equivalent of Q, which was not in the original alphabet. That mismatch, he says, is either fraud or badly misstated dating."}, {"title": "What a forged past does to a person", "body": "The most personal stretch of the episode is Dylan on the emotional cost of discovering the record is fake. Forgery, he says, forces you into a game you never wanted to play, where you can never simply accept anything at face value and always have to account for angles and human nature. He walks through the same shock in relationships, in the legal system, and finally in history itself. Being taught one thing and finding it was built on lies is heartbreaking because you lose the ability to trust even basic things anymore."}, {"title": "History as pre programming for control", "body": "Dylan separates ordinary social lies from narratives built deliberately to steer behavior. His example, credited to a conversation with Crow, is the Gospel of Luke claiming Augustus Caesar taxed the whole world when no historian records the Roman Empire being taxed that way at all. He reads that as seeding the idea of a one world tax, which lands differently in an age of cryptocurrency and digital money that removes the privacy of a physical transaction. He asks the same question about the sexual behavior attributed to Greek philosophers and Roman emperors, much of it drawn from demonstrably forged documents."}, {"title": "The system that props up untalented work", "body": "The two connect Hollywood to academia. Dylan describes a hidden production layer that elevates untalented performers who could never build a following alone, while genuinely talented people can walk away and still succeed. He extends it to social proof and perception, where a manufactured sense of popularity beats being right. Chance takes that as the perfect illustration of mainstream history, which has few merits of its own and would fall apart under scrutiny if an entire academic and pop culture industry were not holding it upright. The paid portion opens with Tacitus and the origin of his manuscripts."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Welcome to Inner Whirled, the new podcast with Dylan Saccoccio and Chance Garton, where we'll be providing deeply researched and well prepared podcasts on Spirit Whirled subjects, the language, symbolism, artifacts and system of the ancient universal priestcraft, all reserved exclusively for our direct supporters.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Episode 4 investigates the widespread prevalence of literary fraud amongst Renaissance Italian humanists, such as Poggio Bracciolini and Petrarch. What would it mean for our view of history, if forgery was the rule, rather than exception, when it comes to the literature of Roman and Greek antiquity? What motivated the fad of fabricating archaic manuscripts? And what does it tell us about the foundations of other institutional paradigms in our modern world, if deception can go unchecked and unrecognized?

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Poggio Bracciolini, Forger by Trade", "body": "Chance walks through the Wikipedia entry on Poggio Bracciolini and reads it back as a rap sheet. The celebrated finds run from De Rerum Natura and De Architectura to lost orations of Cicero and Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria, all of them allegedly fifteen hundred years old, all of them decaying yet still legible, and all of them turned up by one man. He served seven popes, rose to apostolic secretary, and by the sale of a single alleged Titus Livy manuscript bought himself a villa in Florence, while the encyclopedia insists riches never tempted him."}, {"title": "The Preservation Story That Does Not Hold", "body": "The provenance of these texts collapses the moment anyone asks how they survived. Poggio's own letter describes finding Quintilian filthy with mold and dust in a foul and gloomy dungeon at the bottom of a tower, a place he says not even men convicted of a capital offense would have been stuck away. Chance sets that against what is known of medieval scribes, who copied gospels and saints' legends on papyrus, scraped old scrolls to reuse them, and treated destroying pagan work as a holy deed. Monks copying pagan masterpieces onto expensive parchment and then binning them strains belief."}, {"title": "Forgery Was Never Only About Paper", "body": "The pattern runs straight through sculpture and archaeology. Michelangelo built his early reputation faking ancient statues, ageing them with acidic earth, and Lynn Catterson's work points at Laocoon and His Sons, supposedly from around 40 BC and conveniently unearthed in a Roman vineyard in 1506 before the Pope acquired it. Set the equestrian Marcus Aurelius beside Louis the Fourteenth and the centuries between them vanish, with no progression of skill anywhere in the record. Annius of Viterbo went further in 1493, salting marble statues into a dig site and then publicly discovering them."}, {"title": "Petrarch and the Invention of Humanism", "body": "Petrarch sits at the head of the whole fashion. A fourteenth century Catholic cleric and poet, he coined the term Dark Ages, wrote Roman histories including a work on Scipio Africanus, and is credited with discovering a trove of Cicero's personal letters in a cathedral at Verona, a find said to have initiated the Renaissance itself. The mainstream also accepts that he wrote his own letters in perfect imitation of Cicero, in style and in calligraphy. Chance flips the question: was Petrarch writing like Cicero, or were the Cicero letters written in a Petrarchan style all along?"}, {"title": "Why Anyone Plays Along", "body": "Motive gets the same scrutiny as the documents. Italian cities competed hard for prestige, and a Renaissance market that once ran on the bones of saints had turned into a fad for classical artifacts, so demand outran supply and forgery paid in money, clout and renown. Chance argues that men are moved by praise and acceptance more easily than they like to admit, and Dylan adds one word to it, recognition, saying that what closed enclaves and secret societies hand out beats anything you will see in ordinary day to day business. We are easily manipulated by praise and recognition."}]
